claims.text: Reducing dietary saturated fat for at least 24 months reduces the risk of combined cardiovascular events by 17%.
Greater reductions in dietary saturated fat intake result in greater reductions in cardiovascular disease event risk.
Reducing saturated fat intake has little or no effect on all-cause mortality.
Reducing saturated fat intake has little or no effect on cardiovascular mortality.
Reducing saturated fat intake has little or no effect on non-fatal myocardial infarction.
Subgroup analyses show no significant differences in cardiovascular event reduction between replacing saturated fat with polyunsaturated fat versus carbohydrate.

evidence.description: RR 0.83; 95% CI 0.70 to 0.98 across 12 trials with 53,758 participants.
Meta-regression suggested that greater reductions in saturated fat (reflected in greater reductions in serum cholesterol) resulted in greater reductions in risk of CVD events.
RR 0.96; 95% CI 0.90 to 1.03 across 11 trials with 55,858 participants.
RR 0.95; 95% CI 0.80 to 1.12 across 10 trials with 53,421 participants.
Subgrouping did not suggest significant differences between replacement of saturated fat calories with polyunsaturated fat or carbohydrate.

methodologies.name: Random-effects meta-analysis and meta-regression of RCTs
methodologies.description: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials evaluating the effect of reducing and replacing saturated fat on mortality and cardiovascular morbidity over at least 24 months.
conditions: Adult humans with or without cardiovascular disease
Intention to reduce saturated fat intake or alter dietary fats

limitations.text: Data on replacement of saturated fat with monounsaturated fat and protein were very limited.
Effects on total myocardial infarction, stroke, and CHD events were unclear due to very low-quality evidence.
